ORDER AND REASONS

[1] The Applicant, Lirui Shao, seeks a stay of his removal from Canada to China, scheduled for November 16, 2025, until his underlying application for leave and judicial review [ALJR] has been determined or until he is eligible to apply for a pre-removal risk assessment [PRRA], whichever comes first. The underlying ALJR challenges a decision by an officer with the Canada Border Services Agency [CBSA] refusing a deferral of the Applicant’s removal [Deferral Decision].

[2] The motion to stay the Applicant’s removal is granted.

[3] The Applicant is a citizen of China. He arrived in Canada in March 2023 on a visitor visa. Thereafter, he filed a refugee claim based on his fear of persecution from Chinese authorities due to his political opinion. This claim was refused by the Refugee Protection Division (“RPD”) and his appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (“RAD”) was dismissed on November 22, 2024. The RAD found that there was insufficient evidence to establish that the Applicant was a person of interest to the Chinese authorities or that he faced a serious possibility of persecution in China. The Applicant filed an ALJR challenging the RAD decision. Leave was denied on April 30, 2025.

[4] Following his receipt of a direction to report for removal, the Applicant asked the CBSA to defer his removal until he becomes eligible to submit a request for a PRRA. Under s. 112(2)(c)(i) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], the Applicant is ineligible to submit a PRRA application until April 30, 2026.

[5] In support of his deferral request and this stay motion, the Applicant argued that his circumstances have materially changed since the RAD rendered its decision. The Applicant provided new evidence including, among other things:
Letters from family members in China reporting that the police visited or broke into his family’s home in China in August, 2024 and March, 2025 and threatened them due to the Applicant’s political activities in Canada;
Evidence regarding additional rallies, seminars, lectures and other meetings critical of the Chinese government that the Applicant attended in Canada after the RAD rendered its decision;
Information about his friendship and association with a prominent Chinese Communist Party dissident who lives in Canada;
Several online Chinese language media articles and videos that mention the Applicant by name and are critical of the Chinese government [Media Articles];
Information that he joined the Chinese Democratic Party.

[6] This is new evidence that does not raise the prospect of a new or different risk, but has the potential to further substantiate the allegation of risk previously considered by the RPD and the RAD.
I. Stay Test [7] Motions for stays of removal are determined based on the well-established three-part test for interlocutory injunctions: RJR-MacDonald Inc v Canada (Attorney General), 1994 CanLII 117 (SCC), [1994] 1 SCR 311 [RJR]; Toth v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1988), 1988 CanLII 1420 (FCA), 86 NR 302 [Toth].

[10] A higher threshold applies to the “serious issue” branch of the test where the underlying ALJR challenges a decision refusing a deferral of removal. This is because a stay, if granted, would effectively grant the relief sought in the underlying judicial review: Wang v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCT 148 (FCTD) at paras 10–11 [Wang]; Baron v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2009 FCA 81 at paras 66–67 [Baron]. In the context of an ALJR challenging a deferral decision, the applicant must show it has “quite a strong case” to satisfy the first prong of the test: Gill v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2020 FC 1075 at para 21 [Gill]; Baron at paras 66–67.
A. Serious issue – “quite a strong case” [11] The Deferral Decision notes that both the RPD and the RAD assessed the Applicant’s risk and refused the refugee claim. It quotes from the RPD decision, considers the Applicant’s new evidence, and offers comments on that material. It concludes that there is insufficient evidence to support the risk alleged or that the Applicant “is being sought after, inquired about, or wanted by any person, group, or government entity in China.”

[12] I am persuaded that there is “quite a strong case” that the Officer made at least one error that may justify intervention by a court on judicial review.

Irreparable Harm [16] To establish the second prong of the RJR test, the applicant must provide concrete, non-speculative evidence that irreparable harm is likely to occur if the stay is refused: Erhire v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2021 FC 941 at para 65 [Erhire]; Ali v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 751 at para 33.

subthemes.explanation: Observed roles: evidence_fact, issue Display terms: activism, deferral, english, fact, information Evidence spans paragraphs 11-13. This is a deterministic evidence summary, not a legal conclusion.
subthemes.text:
[13] The Deferral Decision states that the Media Articles included in the new evidence “exclude any mention of Lirui Shao or any information pertaining to his political activism.” This finding appears to directly contradict the evidence that was before the Officer and could lead a court to question if the Officer in fact reviewed the Media Articles at all. The Applicant’s motion record includes a Chinese language media article, with a certified English translation, that mentions “Mr. Shao” by name and includes a picture of him at a rally. The article speaks to the development of his anti-Chinese government political beliefs. This article was one of many before the CBSA Officer.

[14] The Applicant also raises a concern with the Officer’s apparent reliance on internet searches of the Applicant. The Deferral Decision states that the Officer searched the Applicant’s name on the internet and that this did not result in “any information about him or his political activism against the country of China.” The decision does not specify the language used to conduct the search. The Applicant points out that online information and stories that name the Applicant are in Mandarin. The Applicant states that a search of the Applicant’s name in English would not be expected to generate results. While it is not apparent how much weight the Officer placed on the results of their independent online searches, the fact that he mentioned it in his reasons suggests it was given some weight. I am satisfied that this too may give rise to a serious issue.

[15] This is sufficient to meet the first part of the RJR test. It is not necessary to address the other grounds of review advanced by the Applicant.
B. Irreparable Harm [16] To establish the second prong of the RJR test, the applicant must provide concrete, non-speculative evidence that irreparable harm is likely to occur if the stay is refused: Erhire v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2021 FC 941 at para 65 [Erhire]; Ali v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 751 at para 33.

argument_evidence.context_text: [17] The Applicant has established there is a serious issue, on an elevated standard, with the Officer’s treatment of the new evidence provided to overcome previous findings that the Applicant would not face a risk upon returning to China.

subthemes.explanation: Observed roles: evidence_fact, issue Display terms: agree, balance, case, china, combination, conclusions Evidence spans paragraphs 14-14. This is a deterministic evidence summary, not a legal conclusion.
subthemes.text:
[17] The Applicant has established there is a serious issue, on an elevated standard, with the Officer’s treatment of the new evidence provided to overcome previous findings that the Applicant would not face a risk upon returning to China. This, in combination with the evidence with respect to the Applicant’s personalized risk provided not previously considered by the RAD, is sufficient to establish irreparable harm: Erhire at paras 67 - 68; Shittu v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2022 FC 1037 at para 26.
C. Balance of Convenience [18] The parties agree, as do I, that the balance of convenience in this case will follow from the conclusions on the first two prongs of the test.

C. Balance of Convenience [18] The parties agree, as do I, that the balance of convenience in this case will follow from the conclusions on the first two prongs of the test.

[19] A stay of removal will be for a limited duration. The short-term harm that will result from the removal of the Applicant to China outweighs the Respondent’s legitimate interest in the orderly and efficient administration of Canada’s immigration laws. The balance of convenience favours the Applicant.
THIS COURT ORDERS that the motion to stay the removal of the Applicant is granted until the earlier of:
a)The final disposition of the underlying application for leave and judicial review; or
b)April 30, 2026, when the Applicant is eligible to file a PRRA.
